title: Lung Cancer: Smoking Carcinogenesis, Driver Mutations, Immunotherapy Breakthrough

content.intro: Lung cancer has a rich and evolving history that spans centuries. The earliest recorded cases date back to the 18th century, with the first documented case by Italian physician Giovanni Battista Morgagni in 1761. However, it wasn't until the early 20th century that lung cancer began to be recognized as a distinct clinical entity. The landmark paper by Alton Ochsner and Michael DeBakey in 1941 highlighted the association between smoking and lung cancer, laying the groundwork for future research. The 1964 report by the US Surgeon General, Luther Terry, conclusively linked smoking to lung cancer, marking a significant turning point in the understanding and prevention of the disease. Key milestones include the discovery of the first oncogene, src, by J. Michael Bishop and Harold Varmus in 1976, for which they were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1989. Famous cases, such as the 'London Smog' of 1952, which caused widespread respiratory issues, further underscored the importance of environmental factors in lung cancer development.

content.intro: Lung cancer pathophysiology involves complex molecular mechanisms and genetic factors. Driver mutations in genes such as EGFR, KRAS, and ALK play a crucial role in the development and progression of the disease. The PI3K/AKT and MAPK/ERK signaling pathways are also implicated in lung cancer, with alterations leading to uncontrolled cell growth and survival. Subtypes of lung cancer, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and small cell carcinoma, exhibit distinct molecular profiles and respond differently to treatments. Genetic factors, such as inherited mutations in the TP53 tumor suppressor gene, can increase an individual's risk of developing lung cancer. Environmental factors, including smoking and exposure to carcinogens like asbestos and radon, also contribute to the development of lung cancer.

content.intro: Lung cancer can present with a range of symptoms, including cough, dyspnea, chest pain, and weight loss. Cardinal symptoms such as hemoptysis and clubbing of the fingers can also occur. The disease can be divided into stages, ranging from stage I to stage IV, with stage IV indicating metastatic disease. Atypical presentations, such as paraneoplastic syndromes and metastatic disease to the brain or bones, can also occur. Clinical evaluation involves a combination of physical examination, laboratory tests, and imaging studies to determine the extent of disease and guide treatment decisions. Accurate staging is crucial for determining prognosis and selecting the most appropriate treatment strategy.

content.intro: Lung cancer diagnosis involves a combination of clinical evaluation, imaging studies, and laboratory tests. The diagnosis criteria include a thorough medical history, physical examination, and diagnostic imaging such as chest X-rays, computed tomography (CT) scans, and positron emission tomography (PET) scans. Laboratory tests such as sputum cytology, blood tests, and tumor biomarkers are also used to confirm the diagnosis. The differential diagnosis includes other lung diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

content.intro: The treatment of lung cancer depends on the stage and type of cancer, as well as the patient's overall health. First-line treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy. Second-line treatment options include targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Pharmacological treatments such as EGFR inhibitors and ALK inhibitors are used to target specific genetic mutations. Non-pharmacological treatments such as palliative care and supportive care are used to manage symptoms and improve quality of life.

content.intro: Lung cancer can cause a range of complications, including respiratory failure, cardiac complications, and neurological complications. The prognosis for lung cancer depends on the stage and type of cancer, as well as the patient's overall health. Prognostic scores such as the TNM staging system are used to predict treatment outcomes. Incidence data show that lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer deaths worldwide.
